title: Reading Hebrew Poetry
summary: How Hebrew poetry works: parallelism, terseness, sound, and imagery; acrostic poems; the kinds of psalms and how the Psalter is arranged; and a glossary of the psalm headings, from selah and maskil to the tune names, with what is known and what is guessed.

sections.h: A third of the Old Testament is poetry
sections.body:
Poetry is not a small corner of the Bible. Psalms, Proverbs, Job (apart from its prose frame), the Song of Songs, and Lamentations are poetry throughout, and so is most of the prophetic writing in Isaiah, Jeremiah, Hosea, Amos, Micah, and the other prophets. Poems also appear inside the stories at moments of high feeling: the song at the sea after the exodus (Exodus 15), the song of Deborah (Judges 5), Hannah's prayer (1 Samuel 2:1-10), and David's lament for Saul and Jonathan (2 Samuel 1:19-27), which the narrator says was taught to the people and written in the Book of Jashar (2 Samuel 1:18). In the New Testament, Mary's song (Luke 1:46-55), Zechariah's song (Luke 1:68-79), and the hymns of Revelation carry on the same tradition, and many scholars think passages such as Philippians 2:6-11 were early Christian hymns. Taken together, poetry makes up something like a third of the Old Testament.

Modern English Bibles show poetry by setting it in indented lines, which older printings did not do. That layout is itself an interpretation, since the ancient manuscripts mostly wrote poetry as continuous text (with some exceptions, such as the song at the sea), but it is a helpful one. When the lines start to indent, the reader should slow down and read differently.

Poetry needs a different kind of attention than prose. It compresses, uses images, and says things indirectly. A reader who takes ‘He will cover you with His feathers’ (Psalm 91:4) as a statement about God's anatomy has misread the kind of writing it is; so has a reader who assumes that because a line is a metaphor it says nothing true. Poetry tells the truth by means of images, and the images are chosen with care.

sections.h: Parallelism: the heartbeat of Hebrew verse
sections.body:
Hebrew poetry does not rhyme and does not depend on a regular meter the way English verse traditionally did. Its most recognizable feature is parallelism: a line is made of two (sometimes three) short parts, and the second answers, echoes, extends, or contrasts with the first.

“The heavens declare the glory of God; the skies proclaim the work of His hands.” (Psalm 19:1). Each part has a subject and a verb and an object, and each word in the first half has a partner in the second: heavens and skies, declare and proclaim, the glory of God and the work of His hands.

The modern study of this feature began with Robert Lowth, an Oxford professor and later bishop of London, whose lectures on the sacred poetry of the Hebrews were published in Latin in 1753. Lowth called the phenomenon parallelismus membrorum, the parallelism of the members, and described three kinds. In synonymous parallelism the second half restates the first, as in Psalm 19:1. In antithetic parallelism it states the opposite: “A gentle answer turns away wrath, but a harsh word stirs up anger.” (Proverbs 15:1). In what he called synthetic parallelism the second half simply completes or builds on the first. Lowth's categories shaped two centuries of study.

In the 1980s several scholars showed that Lowth's scheme, especially the label ‘synonymous’, can hide what the poetry is doing. James Kugel (The Idea of Biblical Poetry, 1981) argued that the second half almost never merely repeats the first; the relation is better summed up as ‘A, and what's more, B’. Robert Alter (The Art of Biblical Poetry, 1985) showed how the second half typically intensifies, narrows, or dramatizes the first: a number increases, a general term becomes specific, a literal statement becomes a figure, or an action moves forward in time. Adele Berlin (The Dynamics of Biblical Parallelism, 1985) described how parallelism works at the level of grammar, sound, and meaning together. Readers can see the movement in Isaiah 1:3: “The ox knows its owner, and the donkey its master’s manger, but Israel does not know; My people do not understand.” The animals move from knowing their owner to knowing where the food is, and then the turn comes: Israel, which should know most, knows least.

The practical lesson is simple and important. When reading Hebrew poetry, do not treat the two halves of a line as saying two unrelated things, and do not build a doctrine on a difference between them that is only the poet varying his words. Ask instead how the second half moves the first: what it adds, sharpens, or turns.

Hebrew poetry is spare. It drops many of the small words that prose uses, such as the definite article, the relative ‘which’, and the object marker, so its lines are short and dense, often only three or four Hebrew words to each half. Translation has to add words to make English sense, and a reader of the English is already reading an expansion.

Scholars have long debated whether Hebrew poetry has meter. Most agree that lines tend to balance in length and that stressed syllables matter, but no system of counting has won general agreement. One pattern is widely recognized: the limping rhythm of three stresses followed by two, which Karl Budde in 1882 identified in Lamentations and named the qinah, or lament, meter, because the short second half seems to break off like a sob.

Sound matters a great deal, though it is mostly lost in translation. Isaiah's song of the vineyard ends with a pair of puns: God looked for mishpat (justice) and found mispach (bloodshed), for tsedaqah (righteousness) and heard tse'aqah (a cry of distress) (Isaiah 5:7). The words sound almost the same and mean the opposite, which is the point. Alliteration, assonance, and wordplay run through the prophets and psalms, and good commentaries point them out.

Poems are also built in larger shapes. A refrain can mark stanzas: Psalms 42 and 43, which many think were once one poem, share the refrain “Why are you downcast, O my soul?” (Psalm 42:5 and 11; 43:5), and Psalm 46 twice repeats “The LORD of Hosts is with us; the God of Jacob is our fortress” (46:7 and 11). An inclusio frames a poem with the same words at start and end, as Psalm 8 begins and ends “O LORD, our Lord, how majestic is Your name in all the earth”. Chiasm, a mirrored order of A-B-B-A, can shape a single line or a whole poem. And the most visible structure of all is the acrostic, discussed below.

sections.h: Images and the language of praise
sections.body:
Biblical poetry thinks in pictures. God is a rock, a fortress, a shield, a shepherd, a king, a warrior, a mother bird, a potter, a husband. Psalm 18 piles these up at its opening: “The LORD is my rock, my fortress, and my deliverer.” (Psalm 18:2). No single image says everything, and the images correct one another; the God who is an immovable rock is also the shepherd who walks with the sheep. Reading well means asking what each image carries in its own world. A shepherd in ancient Israel was not a gentle pastoral figure only but a man who fought lions and bears, and ‘shepherd’ was a common title for kings across the ancient Near East. A horn was an image of an animal's strength, so ‘the horn of my salvation’ means strong deliverance.

The poets also use hyperbole freely. Mountains skip like rams, rivers clap their hands, and a sufferer's bones are all out of joint. These are not claims about geology or anatomy; they are the ordinary language of strong feeling, and prose readers who flatten them into statements of fact make poetry say what it never meant.

Some images come from the older mythology of Israel's neighbors. Psalm 74 speaks of God crushing “the heads of Leviathan” (Psalm 74:14), and Psalm 89 and Isaiah 51 of his defeat of Rahab, a sea monster. Texts discovered at Ugarit (Ras Shamra) on the Syrian coast from 1928 onward, dating to about the thirteenth century BC, tell of the storm god Baal defeating Sea and a many-headed serpent called Lotan, a name closely related to Leviathan. The biblical poets borrowed the imagery of chaos and the sea to claim that the LORD, not Baal, is the true king over every power of disorder, and often tied the image to the exodus, when God divided the sea. Mitchell Dahood's three-volume Psalms commentary in the Anchor Bible (1966 to 1970) pressed the Ugaritic evidence very far; most scholars think he pressed it too far, but the basic connection is widely accepted.

An acrostic is a poem whose lines or stanzas begin with the successive letters of the alphabet. The Hebrew alphabet has twenty-two letters, and acrostics are usually twenty-two lines or stanzas long; even a non-acrostic poem sometimes has twenty-two lines, as Lamentations 5 does, echoing the form. The device is invisible in most English translations, though some Bibles print the Hebrew letter names (aleph, beth, gimel, and so on) as headings in Psalm 119.

Why write this way? The form was an aid to memory, and it also said something: that the subject had been covered from A to Z, fully and in order. In Lamentations the effect is poignant. The poet's grief over Jerusalem's fall in 587 or 586 BC is held within the strictest form in the Bible, as though order were the only way to speak of such chaos. Lamentations 3 intensifies the form, giving each letter three lines, and at its center, in the middle of the book's grief, stands its most famous hope: “Because of the loving devotion of the LORD we are not consumed, for His mercies never fail. They are new every morning; great is Your faithfulness!” (Lamentations 3:22-23).

Some acrostics are irregular. Psalms 9 and 10 together form a broken acrostic, which is one reason many scholars think they were once a single psalm, as the Septuagint treats them. Lamentations 2, 3, and 4 put the letter pe before ayin, the reverse of the later standard order, and the same order appears in some early inscriptions and in the Septuagint text of Proverbs 31, suggesting that both orders were once in use. The Masoretic text of Psalm 145 has no line for the letter nun. One medieval Hebrew manuscript, the great Psalms scroll from Qumran Cave 11 (11QPsa), the Septuagint, and the Syriac all include a nun line, and many modern translations, including the Berean Standard Bible, add it in verse 13: “The LORD is faithful in all His words and kind in all His actions.” Scholars disagree about whether it was lost by accident or added later to complete the pattern.

sections.body:
The Psalter's 150 poems are of several kinds, and knowing the kind helps a reader follow a psalm's movement. The classification most scholars still use goes back to Hermann Gunkel, whose Introduction to the Psalms (completed after his death by Joachim Begrich and published in 1933) sorted the psalms by form and by the setting in life they served. His main types were hymns of praise, communal laments, individual laments, individual songs of thanksgiving, and royal psalms, with smaller groups such as wisdom psalms, songs of Zion, and entrance liturgies (Psalms 15 and 24, which ask who may ascend the LORD's hill).

The individual lament is the most common type in the book, which surprises many readers. A lament usually moves through recognizable parts: an address to God, a complaint (often ‘how long?’), a confession of trust, a petition, and a vow to praise. Psalm 13 shows the whole shape in six verses. It opens “How long, O LORD? Will You forget me forever?” (Psalm 13:1), asks God to answer, and turns: “But I have trusted in Your loving devotion; my heart will rejoice in Your salvation.” (13:5). The turn from complaint to trust is one of the most characteristic moves in the Psalms. Not every lament makes it. Psalm 88 ends in the dark: “darkness is my closest companion” (Psalm 88:18). Its place in Scripture is itself a word to the reader: this, too, may be prayed.

Later scholars refined Gunkel. Sigmund Mowinckel (Psalmenstudien, 1921 to 1924) tied many psalms to worship in the temple and proposed an autumn festival celebrating the LORD's enthronement as king, reflected in the psalms that proclaim ‘The LORD reigns’ (Psalms 93 and 95 to 99); the festival is debated, but his emphasis on worship stuck. Claus Westermann (Praise and Lament in the Psalms) reduced the types to two basic modes, praise and lament, and showed how closely they belong together. Walter Brueggemann (The Message of the Psalms, 1984) described the psalms as moving between orientation (settled trust, as in Psalm 1), disorientation (the collapse of that trust, as in the laments), and new orientation (surprised gratitude after deliverance). These schemes are tools, not boxes; many psalms mix types.

A few psalms trouble almost every reader: the imprecatory psalms, which call down curses on enemies. Psalm 137, after the lament ‘by the rivers of Babylon’, ends with a blessing on whoever dashes Babylon's infants against the rocks (137:9). Other examples are Psalms 35, 69, and 109. Readers have answered in several ways. C. S. Lewis (Reflections on the Psalms, 1958) called the cursing passages terrible and refused to excuse them, yet saw in them the natural cry of people who had been deeply wronged and who took wrong seriously, and he warned readers against assuming their own anger is cleaner. Others emphasize that these are prayers that hand vengeance over to God rather than taking it (compare “Vengeance is Mine; I will repay” in Deuteronomy 32:35 and Romans 12:19), and that they voice the cry for justice of the oppressed. Dietrich Bonhoeffer, in his small book on the Psalms (1940), read them as prayers that Christ himself prays and whose judgment he bore on the cross. Still others think the New Testament's command to love enemies marks a real development beyond them. The psalms are in the canon either way, and they teach at least this: rage can be brought to God in prayer instead of carried out.

The Psalms are not a random pile. The book is divided into five books, each ending with a short blessing, or doxology: Book I is Psalms 1 to 41 (ending 41:13), Book II is 42 to 72 (ending 72:19), Book III is 73 to 89 (ending 89:52), Book IV is 90 to 106 (ending 106:48), and Book V is 107 to 150, with Psalm 150 as the doxology of the whole. Ancient Jewish interpreters, in the midrash on the Psalms, saw a deliberate echo: as Moses gave Israel five books of the law, David gave Israel five books of psalms. Psalm 72 ends with an editorial note, “Thus conclude the prayers of David son of Jesse.” (72:20), though more psalms of David follow later, which suggests that earlier collections were gathered into the book we have.

There are other signs of collections. Psalms 42 to 83 are called the Elohistic Psalter because they use the general word for God, Elohim, far more than the divine name, the LORD (Yahweh); Psalm 14 and Psalm 53 are nearly the same poem, with the divine name in one and Elohim in the other. Groups of psalms are headed by the same name (Asaph, the sons of Korah), and the Songs of Ascents (120 to 134) and the ‘Hallelujah’ psalms (146 to 150) form clear clusters.

Gerald Wilson (The Editing of the Hebrew Psalter, 1985) argued that the final arrangement tells a story. Psalms 1 and 2 form an introduction: the happy person who meditates on God's law and the king whom God sets on Zion. Books I to III trace the Davidic covenant through trouble, until Psalm 89 laments that God seems to have renounced his covenant with David. Book IV, opening with the only psalm headed ‘of Moses’ (Psalm 90), answers with the older faith that the LORD himself is king (Psalms 93 to 99). Book V ends in unbroken praise. Many scholars have followed Wilson's lead in reading the Psalter as a shaped book, though they differ about the details and about how messianic its final shape is meant to be.

The numbering of the psalms differs between Hebrew-based Bibles and those based on the Greek Septuagint and Latin Vulgate, which older Catholic and Orthodox Bibles follow. The Septuagint joins some psalms and splits others, and adds a Psalm 151 (included in Orthodox Bibles). This is why a Catholic liturgical book may call the Shepherd Psalm Psalm 22. In addition, the Hebrew text counts a psalm's heading as verse 1 (or verses 1 and 2), so in many psalms Hebrew verse numbers run one or two higher than English ones.

Most psalms carry a heading, or superscription: a few words before the poem naming a person, a kind of song, musical directions, or an occasion. In the Hebrew text these headings are part of Scripture and are counted as verses. In the Berean Standard Bible used here they are printed at the start of verse 1, so that Psalm 51:1 begins “For the choirmaster. A Psalm of David. When Nathan the prophet came to him after his adultery with Bathsheba.”

The names are the most familiar part. Seventy-three psalms in the Hebrew text are headed ‘of David’, twelve ‘of Asaph’ (50 and 73 to 83), eleven ‘of the sons of Korah’ (42, 44 to 49, 84, 85, 87, 88), two ‘of Solomon’ (72 and 127), and one each of Moses (90), Heman (88, which also names the sons of Korah), and Ethan (89). Asaph, Heman, and Jeduthun appear in Chronicles as Levitical musicians appointed in David's time (1 Chronicles 16:41-42; 25:1). The Hebrew preposition in ‘of David’ (le) can mean by, for, to, about, or belonging to, so the phrase can mark authorship, dedication, or membership in a Davidic collection. Jewish and Christian tradition took it as authorship, and the New Testament cites psalms as David's (for example Mark 12:36 and Acts 2:25). Many modern scholars take the headings as later additions that show how the psalms were being read rather than who wrote them. Conservative scholars reply that the headings are ancient, that David's reputation as musician and poet is deep in the tradition (1 Samuel 16:18; 2 Samuel 23:1), and that the preposition regularly marks authorship elsewhere, as in Habakkuk 3:1.

Thirteen headings tie a psalm to a moment in David's life: Psalms 3, 7, 18, 34, 51, 52, 54, 56, 57, 59, 60, 63, and 142. Brevard Childs, in a 1971 article on psalm titles and midrashic exegesis, argued that these were added by scribes who read the psalms alongside the stories in Samuel, finding the moment in David's life a psalm fitted, and that they invite every reader to pray the psalm as David did, as a person in real trouble before God. Whether one thinks the notes record the original occasion or an early reading of it, they are the oldest commentary on the Psalms that exists.

The technical terms are harder. By the time the Septuagint translators worked, in the third and second centuries BC, the meaning of many had already been forgotten; they translated some by guesswork and simply transliterated others. Modern translations differ accordingly: some translate (‘For the choirmaster’, ‘To the tune of Do Not Destroy’), some transliterate (‘To the chief Musician, Al-taschith’ in the King James Version), and some drop the headings to the margin. J. W. Thirtle (The Titles of the Psalms, 1904) proposed that the musical notes at the head of a psalm really belong at the end of the one before, as a subscript, on the model of Habakkuk 3, whose musical note (“For the choirmaster. With stringed instruments.”) stands at the end of the prayer (Habakkuk 3:19). The theory would explain some puzzles and has a few followers, but it has not been widely adopted. The glossary below gives each term with what can be said with confidence and what remains a guess.

The table gathers the terms that appear in the headings and inside the psalms, in roughly the order of how often a reader will meet them. The right-hand columns separate what the evidence supports from what remains conjecture. ‘Septuagint’ means the Greek translation of the Old Testament made in Egypt in the last centuries BC, whose renderings are the earliest surviving interpretations of these words. Where the English Bible here translates a term, its rendering is given; the tune names in particular are translated in the BSB but transliterated in older versions such as the King James.

Two general cautions apply. First, a term's meaning is often inferred from its root, and a root is a weak guide to a word's use; the terms that are best understood are those the Old Testament also uses outside the Psalms, especially in Chronicles. Second, sermons built on a confident meaning of selah or miktam are building on sand. The honest summary for many of these words is that they are musical or liturgical directions whose sense was lost before the Christian era.

sections.body:
The Psalms have been the prayer book of Israel and of the church for more than two thousand years. Jesus prayed them: on the cross he cried the opening of Psalm 22, “My God, my God, why have You forsaken me?”, and his last words in Luke are from Psalm 31:5, “Into Your hands I commit my spirit”. The New Testament quotes the Psalms more often than almost any other Old Testament book. Athanasius of Alexandria, in his Letter to Marcellinus in the fourth century, described the Psalms as a book in which readers find the movements of their own souls mirrored and are given words for them; Calvin, in the preface to his Psalms commentary (1557), made a similar point, calling the book an anatomy of all the parts of the soul. The Rule of Benedict (sixth century) arranged for monks to pray all 150 psalms every week, and the Book of Common Prayer (1549) spread them over the days of each month.

A few habits help the modern reader. Read a psalm aloud, since these were sung. Notice the parallel halves of each line and ask how the second moves the first. Find the turn, since many psalms pivot on a ‘but’ or a ‘yet’. Pay attention to the images and ask what they meant in their world. Look at the heading, if there is one, and let it set a scene without depending on a guessed meaning of its technical words. And let the psalm say what it says: a lament may complain to God with a boldness that feels almost improper, and that boldness is part of what Scripture teaches about prayer.

Hebrew poetry is also the language of the prophets, of Job, and of Proverbs. The skills learned here carry into the guides on the Wisdom Books and the Prophets, where the same parallelism and imagery bear the weight of argument and oracle.
